subtitle: Turn untrusted JSON into clean, checked data with a DRF serializer.
notes: This deck goes with exercise 5. By the end you should be able to write a serializer with field rules, a check for one field, and a check across several fields.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.text:
Anything a client sends is **untrusted**: a title might be missing, a date might be `"next friday"`, a priority `"URGENT!!!"`. It's like a messy spreadsheet from someone else: check every column before you use it.

A **serializer** is a bouncer with a checklist. Each field is checked on its own, then the whole thing together. You get **clean data** or a dict of **errors**.
slides.notes: Data might come from your own website, but just as well from a script, a typo, an old app version or someone trying to break things. Saving it unchecked gives broken data or crashes.

slides.title: What the tests do
slides.caption: The tests create your `TaskSerializer` with some data, then check the result.
slides.code:
serializer = TaskSerializer(data={"title": "Write docs", "priority": "low",
                                  "due_date": TOMORROW})
serializer.is_valid()
serializer.errors            # the test checks this dict
serializer.validated_data    # and sometimes this one
slides.notes: TOMORROW and YESTERDAY are worked out from today's date when the tests run, as text like "2026-09-27" (YYYY-MM-DD).

slides.title: What they expect back
slides.caption: Error messages must match exactly, full stop included.
slides.notes: Also: no title at all is an error on title; due_date set to None is valid; high priority with a due date tomorrow is valid.

terms.meaning: A DRF class listing the expected fields and their rules.
Field name → list of messages. `{}` when all is fine.
What you `raise` to say "this is not allowed".
The dict of all field values, passed to `validate()`.

slides.title: Tool: a Serializer class
slides.caption: Fields are one line each, like a model. Use it with `data=...`, then `.is_valid()`.
slides.code:
class PetSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    name = serializers.CharField(max_length=20)
    age = serializers.IntegerField(min_value=0)

good = PetSerializer(data={"name": "  Rex  ", "age": "3"})
print(good.is_valid())        # True
print(good.validated_data)    # {'name': 'Rex', 'age': 3}

bad = PetSerializer(data={"age": -1})
print(bad.is_valid())         # False
print(bad.errors["name"][0])  # This field is required.
slides.notes: Three free checks: CharField strips spaces, "3" became the number 3, and every field is required unless you say otherwise. Each message is an ErrorDetail; str(...) gives the plain text.

slides.title: Tools: ChoiceField and DateField
slides.caption: `default=` fills in a missing value. An optional date needs two different options.
slides.code:
class ShirtSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    size = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=["S", "M", "L"], default="M")
    gift_date = serializers.DateField(required=False, allow_null=True)

s = ShirtSerializer(data={"gift_date": None})
s.is_valid()
print(s.validated_data)     # {'size': 'M', 'gift_date': None}

s = ShirtSerializer(data={"size": "XL", "gift_date": "2026-12-24"})
s.is_valid()
print(s.errors["size"][0])  # "XL" is not a valid choice.
slides.notes: required=False means the field may be left out. allow_null=True means it may be sent as None (null in JSON). It's like null and blank on a model. A valid date string becomes a real Python date.

slides.title: Tool: validate_<field> checks one field
slides.caption: DRF calls it after the field's own checks, with the cleaned value. Raise, or return the value.
slides.notes: The name must be exactly validate_ plus the field name, or DRF never finds it. The value arrives already stripped. Forgetting return value makes the field silently become None.

slides.title: Tool: validate(self, attrs) checks fields together
slides.caption: Runs last, with all clean values in `attrs`. A dict puts the error on one field.
slides.notes: For optional fields use attrs.get("name"), not attrs["name"]: a field that was left out is simply not in the dict. Always return attrs at the end.

slides.title: validate_<field> vs validate

left.heading: validate_title(self, value)
bullets: Example: the title is too short

right.heading: validate(self, attrs)
bullets: Gets `attrs`, a dict of all values
Example: high priority needs a date

slides.notes: Ask: does the rule need to look at more than one field? If yes, it goes in validate. A plain string raised in validate lands under non_field_errors instead of on a field.

slides.title: Pattern: check for None, then compare dates
slides.caption: Dates compare like numbers. `and` stops early, so `None` is never compared.
slides.notes: value < date.today() means 'in the past'. None < date.today() would crash with a TypeError, which is why the None check comes first.

slides.title: Your task, step by step

steps.text: Add `priority`: a `ChoiceField` of low, medium, high; default medium
`validate_title`: under 3 characters raises; otherwise return it
`validate`: high priority with no due date raises on `due_date`

slides.notes: The title field is already there, and it already makes tests 3 and 5 pass: CharField is required and strips spaces by default.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: No `return value` or `return attrs` at the end of a check
Only one of `required=False` and `allow_null=True`: you need both
A plain string in `validate()`: it lands under `non_field_errors`
A wrong method name like `validate_titles`: DRF never calls it

slides.title: Where you'll use this
slides.text: A to-do app posts a task with the title `"ab"` and the priority `"URGENT"`. Your API replies **400** with a message for each bad field, and nothing broken is saved.
bullets: Frontend checks are a courtesy; the server's checks protect your data

slides.title: Check yourself
questions: Where does a rule that looks at two fields belong, and why?
Why validate on the server if the frontend already checks?
